skill.name: Can I trust this source?
skill.why: Some texts are written to trick you. Clues show you who to trust.
skill.how: Check who wrote it, what they gain, their evidence, and how recent it is.

beats.say: Before you believe a text, check who's behind it.
Who wrote it? Do they really know the topic?
What do they gain? Sellers want your money.
beats.show: **Buy my snake spray!** Snakes hate it!

beats.say: Do they show evidence, or just say it?
How old is it? Old news can be wrong now.

encounters.frame: Mo saw a snake near the shed. The Proofanna flicked its tongue at two texts about snakes.
encounters.text: TEXT A: A fact sheet from Ranger Mia. She has studied snakes for twenty years. It was updated last week. It says: Most snakes leave people alone. In a count last summer, rangers saw 300 snakes. Not one chased a person. If you see a snake, back away slowly and call a ranger. TEXT B: An ad from Bazza's Snake Spray. encounters.success: Ranger Mia's fact sheet. She knows snakes, it's new, it has evidence, and she isn't selling anything.

options.reason: Bazza wants to sell you spray, and he shows no evidence.

Most children loved it for the first week, but several said it became boring once the battery kept running flat. RoboPup is fun to play with, and it learnt tricks quickly, but buyers should know that the battery is its weak point. Our full results, robot by robot, are printed on the back page.'

encounters.prompt: Put the sources from most trustworthy to least trustworthy.
encounters.success: Fresh test results first, then an older but expert leaflet, then an ad from someone selling the alternative.

items: The town water authority's test results, posted this morning, showing samples from twelve taps across Bluster Rock.
A health department leaflet about floods, printed eight years ago, which says to boil water until tests show it is safe.
An ad from a bottled water company that says, 'Never trust tap water again!' but gives no test results.
body.reason: The results are expert, new and full of evidence. The leaflet is expert but old. The ad gains from fear.

encounters.frame: Players keep twisting their ankles on the new Bluster Rock oval. Tully found two articles that disagree about why.
encounters.text: ARTICLE A, from Grassmaster Turf, the company that laid the oval's new artificial grass. Posted last year. 'Grassmaster Turf is the safest playing surface money can buy. No injuries have ever been linked to our turf, and players everywhere love the bounce. Our turf is made from the finest materials and has been laid at more than two hundred grounds. It stays green all year, even in the hottest summer, and never needs mowing.Clubs that switch to Grassmaster never look back.' ARTICLE B, by Dr Kim Lau, physiotherapist for the Bluster Rock footy club. Posted last week. 'This season, I treated twenty-three ankle injuries from games on the new turf. Last season, on the old grass, I treated six. Most of the injuries happened late in games, and most were on the wing near the clubrooms, where the surface feels hardest underfoot. Several players have also told me their boots grip too tightly when they turn. That is a worrying jump, although it does not yet prove that the turf is the cause, because we also have more players this year. Together with the council, I am now measuring how hard the surface is in different spots, and I will share the results with every club member. Until then, players should wear boots with shorter studs.'
encounters.prompt: Which is the best reason to be careful of Article A?
encounters.success: Grassmaster laid the turf, so it would lose money and business if the turf were blamed.

options.text: Article A is shorter than Article B, so it must leave out lots of important facts.
options.reason: Length doesn't decide trust. A short text can be true. Look at what the writer gains.

options.text: The company that laid the turf would lose money if the turf were blamed.
Article A uses the word 'turf' many times.
options.reason: Repeating a word isn't a reason to doubt a source.

options.text: Dr Lau admits she is still testing, so Article A must be right.
options.reason: Being careful about what she can prove makes Dr Lau more trustworthy, not less.
